clue.text: Bedcover put away shows clumsy patching

indicators.note: clumsy patching is badly done, so the letters of that word are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A bedspread folded and stored reveals some poor mending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clumsy' rearranges PATCHING. The definition plays on two senses: a cap worn in bed covers the head, and a late drink is something you put away.
explanation.definitionFit: A cap worn in bed covers the sleeper's head, and a bedtime drink is one you put away, or swallow.

clue.text: It could be a rare find, if only you could see it

definitions.text: It could be a rare find, if only you could see it

indicators.note: could be signals that the words rare find may become something else when their letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A treasure might be worth finding, if only it were visible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges RARE FIND, and the whole clue describes radiation the eye cannot see.
explanation.definitionFit: Radiation beyond the red end of the visible spectrum, invisible to the human eye.

clue.text: They must listen to some jolly tall stories

definitions.text: They must listen to some jolly tall stories

parts.words: They must listen to some jolly tall stories
parts.note: from the saying 'tell that to the marines', used to scoff at an unlikely tale; 'jolly' is old naval slang for a Royal Marine

explanation.surface: Some people have to sit through very far-fetched yarns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell that to the horse marines' mocks an incredible story, as mounted sailors are an absurdity; 'jolly' is also slang for a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: An imaginary corps of mounted sailors, the people to whom the saying tells you to take far-fetched stories.

clue.text: It's above mere appreciation of a pretty ankle

definitions.text: It's above mere appreciation of a pretty ankle

parts.words: It's above mere appreciation of a pretty ankle
parts.note: the part of the leg just above the ankle, joined to a word for affection, names a youthful infatuation that goes beyond admiring

explanation.surface: Something goes further than just admiring a nice ankle.
explanation.walkthrough: The calf is the part of the leg above the ankle, and the adolescent crush goes beyond mere admiration of a pretty leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A shallow, short-lived infatuation of the young, a teenage crush.

clue.text: "It is quite a three-pipe one ". said Holmes

definitions.text: "It is quite a three-pipe one ". said Holmes

parts.words: "It is quite a three-pipe one ". said Holmes
parts.note: in The Red-Headed League Sherlock Holmes rates a puzzle by how many pipes of tobacco he must smoke to solve it

explanation.surface: Sherlock Holmes remarks on a puzzle needing three pipes of thought.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Red-Headed League, Holmes says 'It is quite a three pipe problem', meaning it needs three pipes of tobacco to think through.
explanation.definitionFit: A puzzle or difficulty needing thought to resolve.

clue.text: Where to make your solution stick

explanation.surface: Advice on where to fix your solution firmly.
explanation.walkthrough: The solver writes the answer in this space in the grid, and the single word means to be inherent, to stick fast in something.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it is this place in the grid, and as one it means to exist inherently, to be fixed in.

clue.text: Fairy of the 17

parts.note: 17 down are the people of Iran, and in their mythology a winged spirit of great beauty is this kind of fairy

explanation.surface: A fairy belonging to some numbered group.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 down is PERSIANS; this is the beautiful sprite of Persian folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: A beautiful winged spirit in Persian mythology, used in English for any graceful fairy-like being.

clue.text: Bank with the Spanish rhyme

parts.note: Dogger Bank is a large sandbank in the North Sea, named in the British shipping forecast
el is the Spanish word for the

explanation.surface: A bank tied up with the Spanish produces some verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' looks financial, but it is the Dogger Bank, a North Sea sandbank familiar from the BBC shipping forecast.
explanation.definitionFit: Comic or badly written verse, crude rhyme.

clue.text: Many a brave fellow ran in front of the cattleman

indicators.note: the word ran is placed ahead of the other pieces, so it leads the answer

parts.note: taken as written
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword standard for many
a brave man is a hero

explanation.surface: Many a courageous man ran ahead of the rancher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' looks like a quantity of brave fellows, but it supplies the Roman numeral C, and 'in front of' puts RAN before C + HERO.
explanation.definitionFit: A ranchero is a Spanish-American rancher, someone who raises cattle on a ranch.

clue.text: A return of fliers a long way off

indicators.note: a return here is a turning back, so the word for the fliers is read backwards

parts.note: the RAF, the Royal Air Force, is Britain's body of military fliers

explanation.surface: A squadron of aircraft comes back from a distant place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return of' turns RAF backwards to FAR, after A. The RAF is the Royal Air Force.
explanation.definitionFit: Afar is an adverb meaning at a great distance.

clue.text: Its experts get cracking at opening time

definitions.text: Its experts get cracking at opening time

parts.words: Its experts get cracking at opening time
parts.note: sounds like busy workers starting when a shop opens; really it is the crime of cracking a strongbox to open it

explanation.surface: Its specialists start work promptly when the doors open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get cracking' means start work briskly, but here the experts literally crack something, and 'opening time' is when they get a vault open.
explanation.definitionFit: Cracking open a strongbox to steal its contents is the craft of a yegg or cracksman.

clue.text: The pale mink coat needs altering. Who'll take it?

indicators.note: a coat that needs altering must be remade, so these letters are rearranged into a new pattern

explanation.surface: A fur coat needs adjusting, but who will accept it?
explanation.walkthrough: 'needs altering' rearranges PALE MINK COAT. 'Who'll take it?' reads as an offer, but defines a compulsive thief.
explanation.definitionFit: A person with a compulsive urge to steal, someone who will take things.

clue.text: Often a dumb sort of game

definitions.text: Often a dumb sort of game

parts.words: Often a dumb sort of game
parts.note: a rhyming parlour game whose best-known version is played in mime, called 'dumb' because the players do not speak

explanation.surface: A remark that some game is usually rather stupid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dumb' looks like an insult, but it means silent: the game's most famous form is 'dumb crambo', where the rhyming word is acted out in mime.
explanation.definitionFit: A Victorian parlour game in which players find rhymes for a given word, often played in mime.

clue.text: Scrooge at chapel

explanation.surface: The miser turns up at a place of worship.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens's miser in A Christmas Carol has this first name; the same Hebrew name, 'stone of help', was often given to Nonconformist chapels in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's miser bears this first name, and it was a common name painted over Welsh and English Nonconformist meeting-houses.

clue.text: Not how James Thomson preferred his loveliness

definitions.text: Not how James Thomson preferred his loveliness

parts.words: Not how James Thomson preferred his loveliness
parts.note: the poet wrote in The Seasons that beauty needs no ornament, being most decked out when left plain

explanation.surface: A comment on the poet's taste in beauty.
explanation.walkthrough: James Thomson's The Seasons says loveliness 'is when unadorned, adorned the most', so he preferred it without the decoration this word describes.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means decorated or embellished, the opposite of the plain beauty the poet praised.

clue.text: Holmes put him at the head of the table

definitions.text: Holmes put him at the head of the table

parts.words: Holmes put him at the head of the table
parts.note: Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote a book about a domineering talker at the breakfast-table, not Sherlock

explanation.surface: Holmes seats someone at the top of the dining table.
explanation.walkthrough: After 5 down, 'Holmes' points to Sherlock, but this is Oliver Wendell Holmes, author of The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruler with absolute power, a despot; Holmes's book title uses it for a dominating talker.

clue.text: Three-dimensional resort with 20's end perhaps

parts.note: a spa is a health resort

indicators.note: perhaps shows the letters of the piece may be arranged some other way

parts.note: the end word of the answer to 20 across

explanation.surface: Describing a solid holiday spot with some feature at its end.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 across is TURN TAIL, whose end is TAIL; 'perhaps' rearranges that to TIAL, after SPA.
explanation.definitionFit: Spatial means relating to space, which has three dimensions.

clue.text: In a word, I ran to the cats' home for them

definitions.text: In a word, I ran to the cats' home for them

parts.words: In a word, I ran to the cats' home for them
parts.note: 'I ran' written as one word is Iran, the old homeland of a long-haired cat breed named after that country

explanation.surface: Someone hurried to an animal shelter on behalf of others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I ran' run together is Iran, formerly Persia, the home country of the long-haired cats and of its people.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of the country now called Iran, and a breed of long-haired cat from there.

clue.text: A near riot could break out in front

indicators.note: a riot breaking out suggests the letters of near riot are broken up and reformed

explanation.surface: A disturbance nearly flares up at the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could break out' rearranges NEAR RIOT; the opening 'A' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Anterior means situated at the front, the opposite of posterior.

clue.text: Sulkiness about deficiency of part of the armour

indicators.note: about means the word for sulkiness goes round the other piece

parts.note: a pet is a fit of sulking
a lack is a deficiency

explanation.surface: A sulk over some shortfall in a suit of armour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts PET around LACK. 'Pet' here is the old noun for a sulk, as in 'in a pet'.
explanation.definitionFit: A placket was a piece of plate armour worn over the breastplate or backplate.

clue.text: How a comet might go into retreat

definitions.text: How a comet might go into retreat

parts.words: How a comet might go into retreat
parts.note: a comet swinging round the sun swings its glowing streamer about; the idiom means to flee

explanation.surface: Asking how a comet would withdraw.
explanation.walkthrough: A comet has a tail, which swings round as it passes the sun, and the phrase is also the idiom for running away.
explanation.definitionFit: To flee or run away from danger, as an animal shows its hindquarters when it bolts.

clue.text: In the result the Romans were victors

indicators.note: In shows the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A statement that the Romans won.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' signals the answer is inside 'RomANS WERe'.
explanation.definitionFit: An answer is the outcome or solution of a problem or sum.

clue.text: Strange meteor situated

indicators.note: strange signals the letters of meteor are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: An odd shooting star is placed somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges METEOR. 10 across is AFAR, so the definition is 'situated afar'.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote means far away, distant from other places.

clue.text: Some of the public annoyed with pollsters ?

definitions.text: Some of the public annoyed with pollsters ?

parts.words: Some of the public annoyed with pollsters ?
parts.note: looks like irritated citizens; really it is a cross (annoyed) section (some of the public), the representative sample pollsters question

explanation.surface: Some citizens are fed up with opinion pollsters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'annoyed' is a synonym for cross and 'some of the public' is a section, and together they make the sample of people pollsters interview.
explanation.definitionFit: Pollsters survey a representative sample of the population drawn from all groups.

clue.text: They don't give a hoot what time of day it is

definitions.text: They don't give a hoot what time of day it is

parts.words: They don't give a hoot what time of day it is
parts.note: the idiom means not caring at all, but read literally it is birds that hoot only at night, not in daytime

explanation.surface: Some people care nothing for the hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'don't give a hoot' means don't care, but these nocturnal birds really do not hoot by day.
explanation.definitionFit: Night birds of prey that hoot after dark.

clue.text: Rainbow goddess isn't 26

explanation.surface: The goddess of the rainbow denies something.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 across is ALL MY EYE; the coloured ring of the eye is only part of the eye, so it 'isn't all my eye'.
explanation.definitionFit: Greek messenger goddess of the rainbow, and the coloured ring round the pupil, which is just one part of the eye.

clue.text: Complete humbug ? One's view entirely!

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses an opinion as utter nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is old British slang for nonsense; read literally it is everything one sees.
explanation.definitionFit: An old slang expression for rubbish or nonsense, and literally the whole of one's sight.

clue.text: Whereon the noughts and crosses player is screened

definitions.text: Whereon the noughts and crosses player is screened

parts.words: Whereon the noughts and crosses player is screened
parts.note: the BBC's still picture shown when no programme was broadcast showed a girl playing noughts and crosses (tic-tac-toe)

explanation.surface: Asking where a player of a pencil game is shown on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screened' sounds like hidden, but means shown on a TV screen: the BBC's long-running test picture showed a girl at a noughts and crosses board.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixed image broadcast when no programmes were on, used to tune television sets.
